strengths: The paper addresses a problem of clear interest to researchers studying predictive uncertainty: improving ID calibration while reducing confidence on OOD inputs. Applying a common partition-based construction to random forests and ReLU networks, without requiring OOD training examples, is useful.

The evaluation has substantial breadth: six synthetic settings, 45 OpenML datasets, and vision experiments. Known-posterior simulations, repeated runs, Euclidean-versus-geodesic comparisons, and per-dataset appendix plots help readers examine the method’s behavior.

The reported improvements are encouraging. On CIFAR-10, KDN reduces MCE from 0.09 to 0.04; on SVHN, it improves OOD AUROC from 0.27 to 1.00. The Gaussian-tail construction also provides an understandable mechanism for returning predictions to empirical class priors at large distances.
weaknesses: Necessary: Narrow the claims of calibration throughout the feature space and against arbitrary OOD datasets. Proposition 4 establishes prior reversion for a fixed fitted model as distance in the Gaussian modeling space diverges, assuming a positive density floor and nondegenerate covariances. It does not establish calibration throughout finite low-density regions. For vision, an OOD input can map into an ID feature region. Also clarify the distance used in this proposition: the geodesic distance in Equation 17 is bounded by 1 and cannot tend to infinity.

Necessary: Distinguish prior reversion from probabilistic calibration. Equation 18 only compares the largest predicted probability with the largest class prior. With priors (0.9, 0.1), predictions (0.1, 0.9) receive zero OCE despite contradicting the target prior vector. Thus OCE does not establish even Equation 1’s stated OOD objective on imbalanced datasets. Revise the terminology and evaluate agreement with the full prior vector; claims of statistical calibration require an appropriate distribution and correctness target.

Necessary: Correct the density interpretation in Sections 3.2–3.3. ReLU logits are piecewise affine, but they are not class-conditional densities; forest leaf predictions likewise estimate class probabilities rather than feature densities. Moreover, selecting only the nearest Gaussian in Equation 5 generally destroys density normalization, and adding a positive constant over R^D in Equation 6 gives infinite total mass. Equation 7 can still define valid normalized class scores, but the manuscript must either present that interpretation consistently or provide a valid density construction.

Necessary: Resolve implementation ambiguities that prevent reproducing the central results. The value or selection procedure for b, which controls the transition to prior predictions, is missing. The grid and optimization objective for k are unspecified. Equations 9–10 estimate Gaussian parameters from samples within each polytope, whereas Algorithm 1 specifies weighted maximum likelihood using other polytopes. Algorithms 2–3 also omit Equation 15’s exponentiation. State which procedure produced the experiments and provide corresponding training and inference details.

Necessary: Make the empirical comparisons auditable and qualify their conclusions. Section 5 defines FPR@95 using 95% precision rather than the conventional 95% true-positive rate; specify the detection score, positive class, threshold rule, and the meaning of Table 1’s uncertainties and repetition counts. Baseline tuning and exposure-data details are also needed. The results show tradeoffs: CIFAR-10 accuracy decreases from 77.78% to 76.84%, and CIFAR-100 OCE remains 0.20 versus OE’s 0.01. These findings support a qualified empirical contribution, but not the broad characterization of consistently well-calibrated ID and OOD predictions.

Optional: Ablations separating the density floor, partition-based weighting, and Gaussian parameter estimation would clarify which components drive the gains. Additional proper scoring rules and measured runtime and memory costs would improve practical guidance.
